doc.title: Bernard Purdie interviewed by Monk Rowe, West Orange, New Jersey, July 30, 2003

chapter: Money and sessions in the sixties
title: Speaking up on dates and overtime
summary: He explains how his face and mouth betrayed him, how he sometimes caused overtime, and the camaraderie of rhythm sections versus horn and string players.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: I had no delivery. I am sorry, I had no delivery. It was bad. It was really, really bad. I’d stop guys, no, no man, no it’s wrong.
I’m sorry. Then I’m saying I’m sorry, but no man it’s not like that.
It must have hit you, like your musical barometer just something would strike you to be so wrong that you just couldn’t resist.

Yeah. I couldn’t. And it happened all the time. See that’s the thing. I get totally upset. I mean my body, my hands and my face said it every time. And when I tried to control it and not say something I’d be sitting at the drums and my face — the guys used to tell me I had more facial —

We’re getting ready to go through this again and he don’t like something. And I tried my best not to say something but it was all over my face. So the arranger or the producer would go, “All right Purdie, what’s wrong?” I said, “Well you asked me. Well you know we really didn’t do that section right, there was some mistakes, and the rhythm wasn’t the right rhythm that should have been played over here, and this shouldn’t have been done here, and this here and this.” And I would rearrange the song. And they’d look at me and the musicians, God dammit Purdie. They wouldn’t say nothing, they’d just look at me. They wanted to kill me.
Were you ever responsible for sending sessions into overtime?

Once in a while. Not often. Because I was one of the first people that would tell ‘em “now people we’ve got to go, we’ve only got five minutes.” Five minute break. Ten minute break. I was back sitting in my chair ready to go. So once in a while it might be me. And then if it was me, even the musicians wouldn’t mind so much. If we went five minutes over, we would not charge them. Or even ten minutes over. We might not charge them. But if we had the string players and the horn players they’re going to get charged no matter what. Because somebody is going to tell. Nobody is — I’m not, or it’s okay, invariably, every time, somebody would go and tell.

That’s very interesting. Do you think there’s a different kind of camaraderie with rhythm section players than there is with — I don’t know, the players who just come in and they get the music set in front of them, and every note is there that they’re supposed to play. There’s not as much creative outlet for them. And I think it affects their attitude to the music.

Yes. Yes it does. And those ninety percent of the time would be the ones that would turn you in. So we couldn’t say that okay it was the string players or it was the horn players, but we know that nobody in the rhythm section did it, because we wanted things to be happening. And even if they made a mistake it didn’t matter because it didn’t affect the rhythm, didn’t affect the sound, didn’t affect the feel. They could bury part of the sound of that mistake but when the rhythm was right everybody else had to go along with the program. And I was right one hundred percent of the time. Not ninety-eight, not ninety- nine. I was right one hundred percent of the time going along for all those years. When I made a mistake everybody knew it. Everybody knew it.
